articles.headline: The Dakota Legislature.
articles.text:
The sixteenth legislative assembly of Dakota met at Bismarck, January 13, and organized as follows:

COUNCIL.

E. A. Henderson, secretary of the council during the session of 1883, called to order the senior branch of Dakota's law-making body. The council then proceeded to the nomination and election of officers.

J. H. Westhover, of Pierre, was elected to the office of president.

A. W. Howard, of Yankton was elected secretary.

Mr. Preston was elected clerk of the council.

Andrew Thompson, Minnehaha, was elected sergeant-at-arms.

Rev. C. B. Austin, Bismarck, was chosen chaplain.

M. D. Kent, Union county, was elected enrolling clerk.

Mr. Pettigrew offered a resolution adopting temporarily the rules of the last council, which was adopted.

The president appointed the following committees:

On Rules—Gamble, Pettigrew, Washabaugh, Walsh and Nickens.

On Joint Rules—Kennedy, Twomey and Wells.

Adjourned until 11 o'clock Thursday morning.

HOUSE

The house was called to order by. T. A. Kingsbury, former chief clerk.

Rev. P. Claire, of the M. E. Church, opened the session with prayer.

First District—Ole A. Helvig, John Larson, Eli Dawson and Hans Myron.

Second District—A. L. Van Osdell, Hugh Langan, J. P. Ward and J. H. Swanton.

Third—J. A. Parshall, Mark Ward, C. E. Huston and H. M. Clark.

Foruth—P. L. Runkell, J. M. Bayard, H. W. Smith and W. H. Riddell.

Fifth—George Rice, John Hobert, J. C. Southwick and V. V. Barnes.

Sixth—J. A. Pickler, Jno. T. Blakemore, Geo. W. Pierce and M. L. Miller.

Seventh—Geo. H. Johnson, M. T. De Woody, Eugene Huntington and F. A. Eldridge.

Eight—A. L. Sprague, E. W. Martin, H. M. Gregg and A. McCall.

Ninth—E. A. Williams, W. F. Steele, Henry W. Coe and Julius Stevens.

Tenth—S. E. Stebbins, P. J. McCumber, Henry Oliver and T. M. Pugh.

Eleventh—Dr. E. T. Hutchinson, W. N. Roach, C. W. Morgan and J. W. Scott.

Twelfth—Donald Stewart, Henry Strong, H. H. Ruger and Patrick McHugh.

The members than took the oath of office, whish was administered by Associate Justice Wm. H. Francis:

Geo. Rice, of Moody county was elected speaker of the house.

Cassius M. Reed, Sully county, was elected chief clerk.

For the remaining offices, the following gentlemen were elected:

Assistant Clerk—J. G. Hamilton, of Grand Forks.

Enrolling and Engrossing Clerk—H. H. Pierce, of McCook.

Assistant Enrolling and Engrossing Clerk—Edward A. Smith, of Dickey.

Sergeant-at-arms—John A. Monroe, of Roberts county.

Watchman—Capt. Fleck of Traill.

On motion of Mr. Williams the rules of the last house and council were adopted for the temporary government of the body.

The speaker then appointed as committee on rules: Messrs. Williams, Johnson, Martin, Pugh and Ward.

Adjourned.
articles.summary: The sixteenth Dakota legislative assembly met at Bismarck January 13 and elected officers of the council and house.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. A Racker from the Rockies
articles.text:
I'm a Buzzard from the Brazos, on a tear;
Hear me toot!
I'm a lifter of the flowing locks of hair;
Hear me hoot!
I'm a Racker from the Rockies,
And of all the town the talk is,
"He's a Pirate of the Pampas,"
On the shoot.

Those who love me call me "Little Dynamite,"
I'm a pet.
I'm a walking, stalking Terror of the Night
You can bet.
By my nickle-plated teasers,
Many a rusty-featured Greaser's
Sun has set.

Sometimes I strike an unprotected town,
Paint it red,
Choke the Sheriff, turn the Marshal upside down
On his head,
Call for drink[s f]or all the party,
And if chinned b[y] any smarty,
Pay [i]n lead.

I'm a coyote of the Sunset, "Prairie Dude,"
Hear my zip!
In company with gentleman I'm rude
With my lip.
Down in front! Remove the nigger!
Or I'll perforate his figure!
I am fly, I am a fighter, I am flip!
—[Stock and Mining Journal.
articles.summary: Comic cowboy-braggart poem reprinted from the Stock and Mining Journal (contains a racial slur, transcribed as printed).

articles.text: During the past twelve or fifteen years there has been a great change in the demand for horses west of the Mississippi river. Formerly breeding was carried on with a view to speed and endurance. Now a large proportion of the breeders throughout the West, recognizing the demand, breed so as to increase size and strength. There has for several years been a steady increasing demand for heavy horses and a corresponding falling off in the call for small ones. The The heavy draft horse stands in about the same relation to work animals that the short horn does to the native Texas steer. Present appearances indicate that it will be many years before the supply of heavy horses will equal the demand. Small work horses are low and a drug upon the market, unless they have some special points of excellence to commend them, more especially perhaps as saddles animals. Our vast ranges covered with untritious grasses afford a good opportunity for investment in this most profitable industry, and we wonder that it is not utilized to a greater extent.—[Stock and Mining Journal.

articles.text: In the decade from 1860 to 1870 there was a serious decrease in cattle, amounting to nearly 2,000,000 head. There was also a very heavy decline in the unmber of swine, while sheep and horses showed a healthy growth. articles.text: A correspondent, writing to The Texas Stockmen from Gillespie county, communicates the information that a young gentleman residing in Western Texas, to recruit his health, being a fine chemist, turned his attention to devising a chemical substitute for branding. The result has been the invention of a chemical compound, semi-liquid, which can be applied by means of an electric brush and a stencil plate. The effect is to turn the hair of the marked portion premanently white. The application causes no pain, and is comparatively inexpensive. The inventor is now endeavoring to modify his compound so as to adapt it to marking white animals.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped range item: A Texas chemist's chemical substitute for hot-iron branding.

articles.text:
The goat is the animal for the ranch and the boundless west, says the Midland Farmer. There will yet spring up a large and profitable business in the
carcasses of the young and the concentrated milk and cheese sent east to the large cities. This will one day find profitable employment to thousands and healthful food to the chronic invalids of city life. The Angora goat possesses all the merits of the common goat, and furnishes a valuable fleece, the use of which is only limited by its scarcness as its beauty is unquestioned. The demand for goat skins for leather is practically unlimited, being alike useful in the manufacture of harness, shoes and gloves, leaving out scores of minor uses. Tanned with the hair on for lap-clothes, ect., the Angora is preferable to tiger, bear, or buffalo for beauty and utility.
articles.summary: Clipped range item: The Angora goat as a ranch animal (Midland Farmer).

articles.text: "No," said the Vermont deacon, "I don't approve of hoss racin', and when another member of the church becomes so godless as to try to pass me on the road comin' home from meetin', I feel it my duty to the church to let out a leetle on the reins just to keep him from puttin' his trust in earthly things."

articles.headline: An Experienced Coal-buyer.
articles.text:
He entered the coal office with a small market basket on his arm.

"Give me a ton of coal."

"Yes sir," replied the coal merchant, "where shall I send it?"

"Oh, just put it in this basket; I'll carry it myself."

"But we have a wagon right here and can send it up at once."

"No; I can carry the coal up easy enough, but you might send the bill up in a wagon."—[Chicago News.
articles.summary: Humorous anecdote about buying coal, from the Chicago News.

articles.text: About 5:30 this morning the peaceful slumbererers of Little Missouri and Medora were awakened by the prolonged whistle of an engine, the cause of which was the discovery of a fire between Bob Roberts and E. G. Paddock's buildings. The whole population turned out, and by strenuous efforts saved most of the stock in the buildings. Mr. Paddock's building was occupied by Gill Kennedy. There was little wind blowing, which was fortunate, as a disastrous conflagration would probably have happened. With considerable difficulty Mr. Roderick's house was saved. Bob Roberts had about two hundred bushels of potatoes stored in his cellar, which were baked in a first-class manner. He estimates his loss at about $1,700. Mr. Paddock's loss is about the same. Both buildings were insured in the Springfield Fre and Marine Insurance Co., of Springfield, Mass. The origin of the fire is a mystery, but it is supposed to be the work of an incendiary. An attempt was made two or three weeks ago to burn these two buildings, but was discovered before any serious damage occurred. The buildings will probably be replaced as soon as the weather will permit. Gill Kennedy's loss will be trifling, as most of his stock was saved. Gill is in Adrian, Mich., but will probably return as soon as he learns of his misfortune.
articles.summary: A suspected incendiary fire early this morning destroyed Bob Roberts's and E. G. Paddock's buildings.

events.date_basis: "this morning" in Thu 15 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Fire destroys Bob Roberts and E. G. Paddock buildings in Medora
events.summary: At about 5:30 a.m. an engine whistle woke Little Missouri and Medora to a fire between Bob Roberts's and E. G. Paddock's buildings; most stock was saved and Mr. Roderick's house was saved with difficulty. Roberts and Paddock each estimated losses of about $1,700, insured with the Springfield Fire and Marine Insurance Co.; the fire was thought to be the work of an incendiary.
events.excerpt: About 5:30 this morning the peaceful slumbererers of Little Missouri and Medora were awakened by the prolonged whistle of an engine, the cause of which was the discovery of a fire

events.date_basis: "two or three weeks ago" before Thu 15 Jan 1885
events.title: Earlier attempt to burn the Roberts and Paddock buildings
events.summary: The paper reported that an attempt had been made two or three weeks earlier to burn the same two buildings but was discovered before serious damage.
events.excerpt: An attempt was made two or three weeks ago to burn these two buildings, but was discovered before any serious damage occurred.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 15 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt plans a large building on his ranch down the river
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt intended to build a large building on his ranch down the river, with E. G. Paddock hauling the lumber. The item does not name the ranch.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt intends the construction of a large building on his ranch down the river. E. G. Paddock will haul the lumber.

events.date_basis: "next week" after Thu 15 Jan 1885
events.title: Marquis de Morès expected home
events.summary: The Marquis de Morès was expected home in Medora the following week.
events.excerpt: Marquis de Mores is expected home next week.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday morning" before Thu 15 Jan 1885
events.title: Packard goes to Bismarck for the legislature banquet
events.summary: A. T. Packard went to Bismarck to attend the banquet given for members of the legislature.
events.excerpt: A. T. Packard went to Bismarck Tuesday morning to attend the banquet tendered the members of the legislature.

events.date_basis: Text gives "January 13"
events.title: Sixteenth Dakota legislative assembly organizes at Bismarck
events.summary: The sixteenth legislative assembly of Dakota met at Bismarck and organized, electing J. H. Westhover president of the council and Geo. Rice speaker of the house.
events.excerpt: The sixteenth legislative assembly of Dakota met at Bismarck, January 13, and organized as follows:

events.date_basis: "on Tuesday" before Thu 15 Jan 1885
events.title: Senate votes to repeal pre-emption, timber culture and desert land acts
events.summary: The paper reported that the senate on Tuesday passed the bill repealing the pre-emption act and also repealed the timber culture and desert land acts.
events.excerpt: The senate, on Tuesday, passed the bill repealing the pre-emption act. The timber culture, as well as the desert land act, were also repealed.

events.title: Black Hills legislators pass through Medora by stage
events.summary: Passengers from the Black Hills included Hon. John R. Wilson and wife, Hon. A. McCall, Hon. H. A. Sprague, Hon. H. M. Gregg, J. A. Bishop, Kane Holland, Hon. G. T. Bennett and Lawrence county sheriff John P. Belding.
events.excerpt: The following were among the passengers from the Hills: Hon. John R. Wilson and wife, Hon. A. McCall
